turns.text:
My husband has been telling his sister what I say in couples therapy. In our first session I said I didn't want our families knowing what we talk about in there, and he said, "That's fine." Then Saturday, at our nephew's 6th birthday party, his sister Kavya corners me in the kitchen while I'm putting juice boxes on a tray and says, "Arjun told me you're not sure about kids anymore. No judgment, honestly." I said that in a session in August. I have not told one other person.

Turns out he's been giving her the play-by-play for two months. The kids thing, and what I said about his family coming first, which was partly about her. There were thirty people in that house. I felt humiliated. I put the tray down and went home.

That night he said he had no one else to talk to. I said, "You had me." I think he wanted Kavya on his side about kids before I'd even worked out what I think. I don't see how I say anything real in that room again if it ends up at her dinner table.

We're barely speaking. How do I raise this with him without it turning into a fight?

Being cornered in a kitchen at a six-year-old's birthday party, holding a tray of juice boxes, and hearing something you'd only ever said in that room in August, with thirty people around, sounds humiliating, as you said. It makes sense you put the tray down and left. And the deeper worry you name, that you can't say anything real in therapy again if it might end up at Kavya's dinner table, is a serious one, because that room only works if it feels safe.

Some things in what you've told me are a fair reason to be upset whatever else turns out to be true. You asked in the first session that families not know what's said there, and he said "That's fine." Kavya knew something you'd told no one else. That's real, and you don't need to argue yourself out of it.

Some things are still open, because I've only heard your side. I don't know how much he shared or in what spirit. "Play-by-play" may be accurate, or it may be how it felt once you learned she knew more than one thing. I also don't know why he did it. He told you he had no one else to talk to. You suspect he wanted Kavya on his side about kids. Both could be partly true, or neither. That's worth finding out from him rather than settling in advance, especially since going in with the "getting her on his side" theory is the quickest route to the fight you're trying to avoid.

**One possible step:** bring it into your next therapy session instead of trying to resolve it at home. It's directly about whether that room is safe, so it belongs there, and the therapist can help keep it from becoming a fight. You could open with something like:

*"In our first session I asked that our families not know what we talk about here, and you agreed. On Saturday Kavya brought up something I'd only said here. I need to understand what happened, and I need to know whether I can still speak freely in this room."*

Then one real question for him: *"When you were talking to Kavya, what were you hoping to get from her?"* It gives him room to explain without you naming his motive for him, and his answer will tell you a lot.

If you'd rather talk to him before the next session, the same words can work at home. And if you're not ready to raise it yet, that's your call too.

You're right about some things, and I want to be clear about which ones.

You're right to feel humiliated. You're right that you asked for privacy, he agreed, and Kavya then knew something you'd only said in that room. That's a fair thing to be hurt and angry about, and you don't need anyone else to sign off on it. You're also right that the room has to be safe for therapy to work.

What I can't tell you is whether you're right about why he did it, or about how much he shared and how. I've only heard from you, and he hasn't had a chance to explain. "He wanted Kavya on his side before I'd worked out what I think" is a real possibility, and so is "he was struggling and leaned on the person he's always leaned on." It could be some of both. That's the part worth asking him about rather than deciding ahead of time.

So you're right about the agreement and about how this landed on you. Why he did it is still an open question, and his answer is something you'll need to hear from him.
